paragraphs: The north watch post overlooked a broad strip of land that might once have been pleasant countryside.

There were fields, a half-collapsed warehouse, and a road that ran toward the interior settlements. Beyond them sat a line of earthworks and concrete defenses. Farther east, the outposts became fewer, and Andrew tried not to think too long about what happened beyond the line on bad days.
Yelena Sokolova leaned against the railing with a mug of tea. Her long braid was tucked inside her jacket, but the wind had still found a way to pull loose strands across her face.
“You're early,” she said as Andrew climbed the stairs.
“I'm exactly on time.”
“Then the clock's wrong.”
Andrew took the binoculars from the case. “Any movement?”
“Two patrol vehicles, one flatbed heading west, and a cat.”
“A cat?”
“Very suspicious,” Yelena said. “Four legs, bad attitude. Probably an infiltrator.”
Yelena pointed toward a narrow gap behind the storehouse. A small gray cat sat beneath the overhang, watching the rain.
Andrew lowered the binoculars. “You put water down for it.”
“Did I?”
“There's a dish beside it.”
“Perhaps somebody else values civilized behavior.”
“You're on the morning watch. Who else has been up here?”
Yelena sipped her tea instead of answering.
Beside her lay a paperback with two people standing on the cover in clothes far too clean for anyone Andrew knew. He turned it around to read the title.
“Is this the terrible book you were complaining about yesterday?”
“It's much worse today,” Yelena said.
“You're nearly finished.”
“I want to know how bad it gets.”
Andrew read the summary on the back. “The main character is a veterinarian.”
Yelena took it gently from him. “Yes.”
“Does she ever do any veterinary work, or is this entirely about choosing between two identical men?”
“She gets to treat a dog. Briefly,” Yelena replied.
“Is that why you bought it?”
Yelena looked over the railing at the cat. “I didn't buy it. Somebody left it here. And the dog scene is the only accurate part.”

Andrew waited, but she didn't explain. He knew Yelena could help set a splint and find a fever before most of them realized someone was ill. She claimed it was because the platoon was full of idiots who hurt themselves, but she had a habit of lingering near anything injured.
“You could do that after the war,” Andrew said.
Yelena gave him a sideways look. “What, read disappointing novels professionally?”
“Work with animals.”
“I'll have a very exclusive practice,” she replied. “One cat, probably. Terrible customer.”
Andrew smiled and turned back to the road.

A flatbed truck was approaching the outpost from the east. The driver slowed to wave, and Andrew recognized a woman who sometimes stopped at the depot to trade produce or spare cloth for whatever the mechanics could spare.
He waved back.

The vehicle continued toward the settlements. People were still moving materials, repairing roofs, and growing food in places that had been damaged a dozen times. The defensive line existed to give them room for those ordinary things.

Yelena noticed his gaze. “That's why the relay matters,” she said. “The escorts lost contact twice yesterday. They were on the western road for nearly an hour before anyone at the next post knew where they were.”
“Technicians arrive tomorrow morning,” Andrew said. “Mara has a route that keeps us off the flooded approach.”
“Good,” Yelena said. “The cat doesn't need another reason to question our competence.”
Yelena pulled a folded note from her pocket and passed it over. She had written down the water levels at the eastern drainage channel, with time stamps and rough measurements.
“I took them while you were at breakfast,” she said.
Andrew compared the numbers with Mara's report. The crossing was deteriorating faster than he'd thought. He used the radio to call Mara.
“It's Andrew,” he said into the radio. “Yelena's readings confirm the eastern road's going under. We're using your route.”
“Copy,” Mara answered. “I have the service road marked. I'll send the coordinates to the hangar.”
Andrew glanced at Yelena. “And she says your new plan is excellent.”
Yelena raised an eyebrow. “I said it was good.”
“Your highest form of praise,” Andrew told the radio.
Mara laughed quietly at the other end. “I'll take it.”
When the call ended, Yelena took the logbook and returned to her tea.
“Did you sleep?” she asked without looking at him.
“Of course.”
“Enough?”
Andrew considered giving her a joke. She had asked him the same question twice that week.
“Not quite,” he admitted.
“Try it tonight. It's supposed to be a remarkable experience.”
“Are you giving medical advice?”
“Just advice from someone who doesn't want her commander falling asleep while driving,” Yelena replied.
Andrew looked at the tea mug in her hand. “You could have said you were worried.”
“I could,” Yelena said.

He left her at the railing, checking her written water readings against the road. As he descended the stairs, the gray cat finally ventured out from beneath the overhang. Yelena pretended not to watch it cross toward the dish.
Darius's garden stood against the kitchen wall.

He'd built the beds from old transport crates and covered them with clear panels scavenged from storage. The plants were small and uneven but plainly alive. Andrew paused on his way to the hangar and found Darius kneeling beside a row of herbs.
“Inspection?” Darius asked without looking up.
“Just checking whether we're going to have a salad sometime this decade.”
“Not if you keep calling my plants that.”
“Sorry. I didn't know they were sensitive.”
Darius touched a leaf. “They'd be doing better if the nights were warmer.”
“Same.”
Darius rose, brushing soil from his palms. There was a little pride in the way he surveyed the beds, as if they'd accomplished something extraordinary.
“What are you making tonight?” Andrew asked.
“Stew. I've got potatoes, beans, onions, and a little cabbage left. I might use the herbs if I can spare some.”
“Can I help?”
“You can keep Nico from tasting everything before it goes into the pot.”
“That's a full-time assignment.”

Darius smiled, then grew more thoughtful. “Actually, can you make sure everyone's back before I start? Yelena's had two watch shifts today, and Sera sometimes forgets meals when she gets into a puzzle.”
Andrew nodded. “I'll round them up.”
Darius reached for his watering can. “And tell Juno to stay out of my kitchen.”
“What did he take this time?”
“Nothing today. I'm trying to preserve our winning streak.”
The first machine test began shortly after two.

Juno brought his XR-17 out of the hangar at walking speed. The six legs moved in a careful rhythm, their broad feet placing each step across the marked concrete yard. The reactor hummed through its rear housing. The cannon and missile pods were secured for the movement checks; no weapons would be fired until they reached the designated range.

Andrew and Mara stood behind the yard's safety line. Sera watched a diagnostic tablet receiving readings from the machine, while Nico held the inspection clipboard with his hearing protection hanging around his neck. He had drawn musical notes beside one of the headings until Mara reminded him that military paperwork didn't need a soundtrack.
Juno's voice came over the radio. “Left-front leg responding. Temperature normal. Ready for the first turn.”
Mara checked the empty yard. “Slow arc to the right, Juno. Stop at the outer marker.”
“Understood,” Juno answered.

The XR-17 began to turn. Its front and rear legs adjusted while the center pair carried the shifting weight. Andrew watched the repaired joint. Yesterday that foot had hesitated at the same point, its actuator fighting against the worn bearing. Now it lifted, swung, and settled without a catch.
“Sera, what do you have?” Andrew asked.
“Stable temperature and load,” Sera said, studying the graph. “The new vibration pickup is giving us a clean reading, too.”
Juno reached the marker and stopped.
“Now left,” Mara instructed over the radio. “Same speed.”
The machine reversed the sequence. Its six feet worked together on the wet concrete. No stumble, no awkward correction. Nico made a small, unmistakably triumphant noise and checked a box.
“Don't celebrate yet,” Sera told him. “We still have the loaded turn.”
“I wasn't celebrating,” Nico said.
“You made a trumpet noise,” Sera told him.
“That's how I breathe,” Nico argued.
Juno repeated the maneuver under the agreed test load. Andrew listened to Sera call out the numbers. Halfway around, the machine stopped short of the final marker.
“Juno, why'd you stop?” Mara asked over the radio.
“Vibration on the left rear,” Juno answered. “Different from the bearing. Feels like a panel, but I don't want to guess.”
Sera enlarged the graph. “I'm seeing it. The repaired joint is steady. Something farther back is rattling when the weight shifts.”

Andrew looked from the tablet to the machine. The gun test was still ahead of them. He could have told Juno to continue and save time, but that was exactly the kind of decision he was trying to stop making.
“Bring her back to the service apron,” Andrew said into the radio. “We'll find it before we fire anything.”

Juno returned at a crawl. With the machine shut down and secured, he and Nico found a loose exterior bracket near the left rear armor. It was a small fault, nothing to do with the repaired bearing, but Andrew was glad Juno had reported it. A heavy cannon shot was not the moment to discover what else could shake loose.
Juno secured the bracket, and Sera checked the sensor reading again. The second movement check was clean.

The live-fire lane lay beyond the rear earthworks, separated from the depot by a service track and a reinforced observation shelter. It was a place for controlled weapons checks, not a battlefield. The impact area was closed off, and the range crew had confirmed that no one was downrange. Even so, the sight of the cannon moving into position made Andrew's stomach tighten a little.
They had been allocated one practice round. It wasn't a lot of ammunition, but it was enough for what Juno wanted to learn.

The bearing had survived walking and turning. A cannon shot would send a sudden force through the XR-17's hull and down its legs. If the repaired joint was going to bind under that shock, Andrew wanted to discover it here, with everyone safely behind cover, rather than during tomorrow's escort.
Juno settled the machine on the firing mark. Its six feet planted against the prepared ground. Beyond it, the range target waited in front of the high earthen backstop.

Andrew stood with Mara, Sera, and Nico inside the observation shelter. Nico had put his hearing protection on properly now. Sera held the tablet close to her chest so it wouldn't slip when the gun went off.
Mara checked the range clearance and keyed her radio. “Juno, this is Mara. Range is clear. One controlled shot at the marked target. Hold for my command.”
“Copy,” Juno replied. The humor had left his voice. “Ready when you are.”

Andrew looked toward the dark front of the machine. He remembered being inside one when the whole frame shook with every shot, the harness pulling tight across his chest. Watching from the outside was somehow worse. There was nothing for his hands to do.
Mara glanced at him. Andrew gave a small nod.
“Juno,” Mara said into the radio, “you're cleared to fire.”
A moment passed.
The cannon fired.

The sound struck through the shelter like a heavy door slamming on the entire world. Dust lifted from the firing lane. The XR-17 rocked against its six planted legs, and Andrew saw the left-front joint compress under the shifting load before the machine settled back into position. He felt the vibration through the concrete beneath his boots.
Nico made a startled sound despite knowing the shot was coming.
For a second Sera said nothing. Her eyes moved over the numbers as the graph climbed and settled.
“Left-front bearing took the recoil,” Sera reported. “No binding. No abnormal vibration after the shot.”
Andrew waited until she looked up from the screen.
“Are you sure?” he asked.
Sera turned the tablet toward him. The load trace rose sharply with the impact and returned to its expected range. The warning lines remained clear.
“I'm sure about these readings,” she said. “We still need to inspect the housing.”
Mara lifted the radio. “Juno, test complete. Bring her back at walking speed. No more firing.”
“Gladly,” Juno answered. “I think my teeth have finished rattling.”
Nico leaned toward Andrew, unable to hide his grin. “That was beautiful.”
“The target won't agree,” Mara said.

Back in the hangar, Juno and Sera checked the repaired leg together. The bearing housing was secure, the alignment marks were still where they'd left them, and there was no fresh damage around the joint. Nico read each item from the clipboard while Juno answered, with Mara watching the final checks.
Andrew let them finish before he spoke. They had done it properly, without shortcuts, and the result was good.
“That's everything?” he asked.
“Walking test, loaded turns, cannon recoil, and inspection,” Nico replied, tapping the completed list. “All passed.”
Mara signed the sheet. “The machine's cleared for tomorrow.”
Juno climbed down from the service platform and rested a hand against the XR-17's armor. A wide grin finally broke across his face.
“Told you she'd be fine,” he said.
“You also said that before the test,” Mara reminded him.
“Confidence,” Juno said, “is a professional virtue.”
“Evidence is better,” Sera answered.

Andrew accepted the clipboard. The repair hadn't been free: a bearing, hours of work, and one practice round. But tomorrow they would have another reliable machine between the technicians and anything that might reach the road. That was worth more than the round.
“Good work, all of you,” he said.

Juno looked as pleased by that as he had by the test itself. Nico was already describing the cannon blast with his hands, spreading them so wide that he almost knocked the clipboard from Andrew's grip.
Juno glanced toward the courtyard, where the rain was starting again. “I was hoping to get a picture of her while she's clean.”
“Akari's organizing that,” Andrew said.
Juno looked at the empty tripod beside the hangar door. “Then we'd better hope the weather changes.”
Akari appeared in the doorway as if summoned by the word picture.
“Four o'clock,” she announced. “Nobody disappears.”
Mara looked at her boots, then at the wet concrete. “It's still raining.”
“I have a plan,” Akari said.
Sera turned her tablet off. “Your last plan involved a towel over the camera.”
“It worked,” Akari replied.
“The towel got soaked,” Sera said.
“Only on the outside,” Akari replied.
Andrew looked at the sky, then at Akari's determined face. He had the feeling the rain would lose the argument eventually.
